subject: Archaeology
title: The Khmer Empire: Angkor's Slow Decline
description: A 60-second lesson on The Khmer Empire: Angkor's Slow Decline.

hook.text: The Khmer Empire built Angkor Wat and ruled Southeast Asia for 600 years. Then the jungle swallowed their capital.

buildup.text: At its peak, Angkor was the largest pre-industrial city on earth — a million people supported by a vast water management network.

discovery.text: LiDAR revealed the true extent of Angkor in 2012: a sprawling urban landscape extending far beyond the temple complex.

twist.text: Climate studies show severe droughts in the 14th and 15th centuries destroyed Angkor's water system.

climax.text: Thai invasions delivered the final blow in 1431. But the collapse was already underway.

punchline.text: The world's largest city ran on water. When the rain stopped, so did the empire.

quiz.question: What was the primary cause of Angkor's decline?
options: A plague carried along trade routes from China
Severe droughts destroyed the water management system the city depended on
Internal religious conflict led to civil war and abandonment

details.summary: The Khmer Empire centered at Angkor declined gradually from the 14th century onward as its massive water management system failed under prolonged drought and flooding. Combined with military pressure from Thai kingdoms, the capital was eventually abandoned by the 15th century.
details.whyItMatters: Angkor's decline shows how infrastructure failure can destroy a civilization. The Khmer water system that enabled a million-person city became a vulnerability when climate patterns changed — a warning for modern infrastructure-dependent societies.
takeaways: Angkor's water management system failed under climate stress
Prolonged drought and flooding damaged critical infrastructure
Military pressure from Thai kingdoms accelerated the decline

faq.question: How did Angkor's water system cause its decline?
faq.answer: The Khmer built an enormous network of reservoirs, canals, and rice paddies that supported a population of perhaps one million. When monsoon patterns shifted — producing both severe droughts and catastrophic floods — the system could not cope, and food production collapsed.

faq.question: Was Angkor truly abandoned?
faq.answer: The political center shifted south to Phnom Penh, but Angkor Wat itself was never completely abandoned. Buddhist monks maintained the temple continuously. LiDAR surveys show that suburban areas around Angkor remained occupied long after the court departed.
